title: The news
hookLine: read the news and pray for the people in it
tomorrow: a stranger online calls Sofia trash. what does she type back?

cards: A push alert at lunch. Another at dinner. A flood somewhere, a fire somewhere else, faces on a screen for a few seconds and then gone.
Two easy responses: go numb, or stop looking. Some grandmothers have a third. They watch the evening news with a rosary in hand, praying for whoever comes on the screen.
Does it help anyone? The question underneath is older: who are those people to me?

teach.h: JOYS AND HOPES, GRIEFS AND ANXIETIES.
teach.b: The Second Vatican Council opened one of its documents with an answer.
The joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of people today, especially the poor and all who suffer, are the joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of the followers of Christ.
Nothing truly human, it says, fails to echo in their hearts.

Another Council document starts from the other end: all peoples are one community, with one origin, because God made the whole human race. So the people in the headline aren't strangers. They're family, a long way off.

teach.h: ALL THE MEMBERS SUFFER WITH IT.
teach.b: Paul gives the picture, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "if one member suffer any thing, all the members suffer with it."
Praying the news is letting that ache in and turning it toward God, and sometimes toward a gift or a hand. A neighbor tradition uses nearly the same picture.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported in a hadith to have said that believers, in their love, mercy and kindness to one another, are like one body: when one part aches, the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever.
Catholics and Muslims share that image of a body that can't rest while one part hurts. The difference is honest.

Paul's body is the body of Christ, which Catholics believe is joined to Christ himself; the hadith speaks of the believers' mercy to one another, with no such claim. Neither ranks anyone. Both refuse to look away.

how: Catholics pray for the world in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, and some keep a habit of praying for the people in the day's news, often with the rosary.

games.q: a classmate scrolls past a story about families fleeing a war and says 'not my problem, I don't know them.' what's today's answer?
o: the Church calls all peoples one community, with one origin.
he has a point; prayer is mostly for the people close to you.
only people who share one faith are really connected.
games.why: Nostra Aetate: one community, one origin. Gaudium et Spes: the griefs of people today are the griefs of Christ's followers. family, a long way off.

practice: Open one headline, or bring back one you saw today, and rest your eyes on a single face or place in it. Stay there for a few breaths, as if it were family a long way off.
If you pray, you can pray for them by name or by place; if not, simply hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: The news. The day's headlines, read as news about family: the people in them, held in prayer.

orig.note: Latin: joy and hope. the first words, and the name, of the Council's document on the Church in the world today.

carryVoice: Your line: pray the news. The people in the headline belong to one human family. Peace to you.
